title: Part Observation, Part Invention
paragraphs: It is tempting to treat The Starry Night as a transcription of what Vincent van Gogh saw from his window at the asylum in Saint-Remy. That reading treats a complex work as a simple document. The museum that owns it, the Museum of Modern Art in New York, encourages a subtler reading. The painting, made in mid-June of eighteen eighty nine during the roughly twelve months Van Gogh spent there, rests on his direct observation as well as on his imagination, memories and emotions.

The evidence for that mixture is visible in the picture. Close looking rewards patience: the brushwork, the colour and the composition all serve the mood more than the map. The morning star glows as it did before dawn; Van Gogh described seeing it from his window in a letter to his brother Theo. The village below, by contrast, is an invention: it belongs to the landscape of memory and imagination rather than to the view outside. The sweeping cypress in the foreground links the two realms, rising from the sleeping earth into the restless sky.

Why does this blend matter? Partly because it shows that the painting is not a record of a place so much as a record of an experience. Viewers who look for a photographic match with the real sky will miss the point; those who look for feeling will find it in every swirl. That is perhaps why the image has outlived so many more literal depictions of the night. No single explanation can exhaust a picture like this.
